jura-039.title: Sea level climbs, then falls back
jura-039.text: Sea level swung by several tens of metres across the Early Jurassic. It stayed near today's level in the Hettangian and Sinemurian, then rose several tens of metres in the late Sinemurian–Pliensbachian. It fell back to near present levels by the late Pliensbachian. During the latest part of the Toarcian the sea level again dropped by several tens of metres.

jura-040.title: Saltriovenator, the oldest known ceratosaur
jura-040.text: The oldest known ceratosaur, Saltriovenator, comes from the early Sinemurian of Italy, 199.3–197.5 million years ago. It belongs to the earliest averostran theropods, which appeared in the Early Jurassic. Ceratosauria originally included the Coelophysoidea and Dilophosauridae as well, which implied a much earlier divergence of ceratosaurs from other theropods. Abelisauroids flourished in the Southern Hemisphere in the Cretaceous. Their origins go back to at least the Middle Jurassic, with the earliest remains from Australian and South American deposits dated to about 170 million years ago.

jura-044.title: Lyme Regis mudstones yield the armored Scelidosaurus
jura-044.text: The cliffs between Lyme Regis and Charmouth give up complete skeletons. The Charmouth Mudstone yields the armoured dinosaur Scelidosaurus, plus plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs, along with large numbers of exceptional fish and a diverse insect fauna. It dates to the Early Jurassic (Sinemurian–Pliensbachian). It is best exposed in those cliffs but extends north to Market Weighton in Yorkshire and underground in the East Midlands Shelf and Wessex Basin.

jura-051.title: Volcanoes erupt across southern Sweden
jura-051.text: Small volcanoes dotted southern Sweden. Volcanism in central Skåne had its first and main phase from the late Sinemurian to the Toarcian, about 191 to 178 million years ago. It was a field of cinder cones with Strombolian eruption styles. A lahar, a volcanic mudflow, at Korsaröd buried Early Jurassic wood, pollen and spores, preserving them exceptionally well. The volcanism was linked to the break-up of Pangea, and so is analogous to the much more voluminous Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts of Southern Africa.

jura-053.title: The first pliosaurs enter the seas
jura-053.text: Short-necked sea hunters entered the fossil record about 190 million years ago. These were the pliosaurs, short-necked plesiosaurs. Many groups of primitive sea invertebrates appeared about the same time, and sponge reefs developed extensively. Thalassophonea, the best-known pliosaur subclade, had crocodile-like short-necked forms with large heads and massive toothed jaws. Pliosaurs range from 4 to 10 meters or more in length.

jura-079.title: The first true Ginkgo trees appear
jura-079.text: Ginkgo has a long pedigree. The earliest members of the genus, with ovule and pollen organs like the living species, appear in the Middle Jurassic of the Northern Hemisphere. Ginkgoales were among the most important parts of Eurasian Jurassic floras. Other Jurassic lineages had Ginkgo-like leaves but differently arranged reproductive structures from living and fossil Ginkgo. Today the genus is represented by a single species, Ginkgo biloba.

jura-086.title: Long-isolated terranes dock with North America
jura-086.text:
Western North America grew by collecting pieces of other places. The Alexander and Wrangellia terranes, long isolated in Panthalassa, were accreted to it in the Middle Jurassic. The Cache Creek Ocean probably closed at the same time, and the Stikinia terrane was also added during the Jurassic.

The first terrane collisions on the western edge came earlier, in the early Triassic, when the Quesnel, Cache Creek and Stikine terranes combined to form the Intermontane Superterrane. The likely order of arrival was Yukon-Tanana, Quesnel, Cache Creek and Stikine. It is also possible that these terranes were assembled as one unit before reaching North America.

jura-089.title: Carnosaurs join the ranks of predators
jura-089.text: Carnosaurs first appeared in the Middle Jurassic around 174 Ma. Their last definite family, the carcharodontosaurids, died out about 90 Ma. Distinctive characteristics include large eye sockets, a long narrow skull, and a thigh bone (femur) longer than the shin (tibia). The largest carnosaurs can reach up to 10 meters in length. The group once held more: most former carnosaurs, such as the megalosaurids, the spinosaurids and the ceratosaurs, were reclassified as more primitive theropods.

jura-091.title: Dinosaur tracks and bones on the Isle of Skye
jura-091.text: Skye's Trotternish peninsula holds rare traces of Middle Jurassic dinosaurs. Rocks there, about 174-166 million years old, preserve footprints and bones. Bones of large theropods, sauropods and thyreophorans have been found, with footprints of all three at Staffin Bay, Duntulm and Brother's Point. That matters because dinosaur fossils are scarce from the Early and Middle Jurassic, though by the Late Jurassic dinosaurs were dominating the planet.

jura-098.title: Megalosaurids appear in Europe
jura-098.text: The first great predators of the tetanuran line appeared in Europe. Megalosaurids, the oldest radiation of tetanuran theropods, first appeared there during the Bajocian, around 170 Ma. By the late Middle Jurassic, megalosaurines were already among the largest land predators. The earliest members of the Tetanurae themselves appeared during the late Early Jurassic or early Middle Jurassic.

jura-100.title: Iberia slides away from Europe
jura-100.text:
Iberia took a long time to break free. From 170 to 120 Ma it slid more than 200 km sideways past Europe as it rifted away from the Grand Banks. Rifting had begun earlier: in the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic there were two stages, with extension and subsidence, on Iberia's western margin.

In the Late Jurassic the Iberian microcontinent broke from the European plate, and the Valais Ocean opened between them. In the same period Africa started moving east and the Alpine Tethys opened.

jura-144.title: Juramaia, a shrew-like start to the placental line
jura-144.text:
A shrew-like animal from China is the oldest known eutherian. Juramaia sinensis, dated to about 160 Ma, sits closer to the ancestry of placental mammals than to marsupials.

It also poses a puzzle. The earliest proposed placental mammal, Juramaia, is Jurassic, yet the earliest known monotreme, Teinolophus, is Cretaceous, even though placentals are more derived and should appear after monotremes. Recalibrations of genetic and morphological diversity rates have suggested a Late Cretaceous origin for placentals and a Paleocene origin for most modern clades. The fossil and the calculations still disagree.

jura-160.title: Cimmeria finally docks against Laurasia
jura-160.text:
A drifting sliver of crust finally ran into a continent. About 150 Ma Cimmeria collided with Laurasia and stalled, and the ocean floor behind it buckled under, forming the Tethys Trench. Late Jurassic collisions of Cimmerian fragments with Eurasia are recorded in Greece's Hellenic orogeny.

Cimmeria, a piece of shelf, had traveled north over about 60 million years, pushing the floor of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean under the eastern end of northern Pangaea. The Neo-Tethys Ocean formed between Cimmeria and Gondwana, directly over where the Paleo-Tethys had been.

jura-168.title: The Arctic Ocean begins to open
jura-168.text: The Arctic Ocean opened from around 148 to 70 Ma, accompanied by the High Arctic Large Igneous Province. It was a result of Pangaea's breakup across the Jurassic–Cretaceous, which opened the Amerasian Basin. As the Atlantic and Arctic oceans opened during the Mesozoic and into the Cenozoic, the Arctic Region went through several stages of rifting, sedimentation and magmatism. The flood basalts in the Canadian Arctic Islands are similar to the Columbia River flood basalts of the Pacific Northwest.

cret-011.title: Raptors appear: the first dromaeosaurs
cret-011.text: The 'raptors' arrive at the start of the Cretaceous. The first dromaeosaurs are placed there, around 143 million years ago. Teeth possibly from dromaeosaurs are known from the Jurassic, but no body fossils until the Cretaceous, in the Early Cretaceous (145-140 million years ago). The family survived until the Maastrichtian, 66 Ma. Dromaeosaurs belong to Coelurosauria, in the clade Paraves, together with avialans and troodontids.

cret-002.title: Shark-toothed giants spread across the globe
cret-002.text:
Giant predators spread across the continents. Large carcharodontosaurids dispersed worldwide in the Early Cretaceous, reaching Africa, North America and South America. The dispersal may have passed through Apulia in Italy, then joined to Africa by a land bridge, as dinosaur footprints there suggest.

With the spinosaurids, they were the largest predators of the early and middle Cretaceous throughout Gondwana, with species also in North America, Europe and possibly Asia. Acrocanthosaurus, Giganotosaurus, Mapusaurus, Carcharodontosaurus and Tyrannotitan all rivaled Tyrannosaurus and Spinosaurus in size.

cret-008.title: The Eromanga Sea floods inland Australia
cret-008.text: An inland sea drowned much of Australia during the Early Cretaceous. The Eromanga Sea flooded large parts of what is now Queensland and Central Australia at least four times, and it was home to the giant pliosaur Kronosaurus. The present-day Winton Formation represents remnants of the river plains that filled the basin the sea left behind.

cret-020.title: Mjølnir: a bolide hammers the Barents Sea floor
cret-020.text: A bolide about 2 km wide struck the floor of what is now the Barents Sea off Norway. It left a 40-km crater, dated to 142.0 ± 2.6 million years ago. In 2006 Swedish geologists found indications of a tsunami that flooded the Swedish southern coast about 145 million years ago. They speculated it was associated with the Mjolnir impact.

cret-022.title: Orb-weaver spiders appear, spinning wheel-shaped webs
cret-022.text: Spiders learned to build traps in the sky. Orb-weaver spiders, builders of wheel-shaped webs, appeared around 140 Ma. The orb-web consists of a frame and supporting radii overlaid with a sticky capture spiral. Because orb-webs absorb the impact of flying prey, orbicularian spiders became the dominant predators of aerial insects in many ecosystems.

cret-033.title: The Faraoni Event brings another warm pulse
cret-033.text: The Early Cretaceous warmed in a series of pulses. The middle Hauterivian Faraoni Thermal Excursion followed the Weissert event in that series. It was a hyperthermal event induced by flood basalt volcanism. A minor oceanic anoxic event, mostly recorded around the Atlantic, has been proposed for the Hauterivian.

cret-035.title: The first anglerfish appear
cret-035.text: The first anglerfish appeared about 130 Ma. They are ray-finned fish of the order Lophiiformes. Their oldest fossils are younger than that, from the Eocene of the Monte Bolca formation in Italy, and they already show diversification into the modern families.

cret-040.title: Colombia's Paja shales preserve sea reptiles
cret-040.text: Colombia holds the world's most complete record of Early Cretaceous marine reptiles. The IUGS lists the Paja Formation as a geological heritage site for it. Its shales and mudstones were laid down in an anoxic, warm, shallow sea that covered much of present-day Colombia. The formation dates from the late Hauterivian to the late Aptian. The Selli event of the early Aptian, about 120 Ma, was active while its black shales were being deposited.

cret-042.title: Tookoonooka: a crater buried deep in Australia
cret-042.text: A crater 55–66 km across lies buried deep in the Eromanga Basin of Australia. Shocked quartz in drill core proved its impact origin, and the nearby Talundilly structure may be its twin. The impact occurred during deposition of the Cadna-owie Formation, whose age is estimated variously at 123-133 Ma or 115-112 Ma, so sources differ on the date. Tookoonooka is associated with several small oil fields.

cret-047.title: Las Hoyas preserves a Spanish wetland in stone
cret-047.text: A freshwater wetland in Spain preserved its dead with unusual care. The limestones at Las Hoyas, about 125 Ma, hold dinosaurs and many enantiornithine birds exquisitely, and Montsechia, one of the oldest flowering-plant macrofossils. Microbial mats may be responsible for preserving the soft tissue in many fossils, such as the crest of Pelecanimimus. Charophyte and ostracod assemblages constrain the age to the Late Barremian.

cret-044.title: Stressed forests pour out resin, and amber piles up
cret-044.text: Trees bled resin on a vast scale. Heat-driven storms, hurricanes and wildfires plus insect damage made them produce huge amounts of it from 125 to 75 Ma. The Cretaceous Resinous Interval began roughly 125 million years ago, during the Barremian age. By the Early Cretaceous, amber formed in concentrations matching or exceeding those of the Carnian. After the interval, in the Maastrichtian, amber was widely distributed but scarce and rarely held bioinclusions.

cret-050.title: Thalattosuchian sea crocodiles fade away
cret-050.text: The marine crocodile relatives that were abundant in the Jurassic faded in the Early Cretaceous. Thalattosuchians became scarce and mostly tropical, with their last records in the Aptian. The clade was mostly marine, lived from the Early Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous and had a cosmopolitan distribution. They are not members of Crocodilia, and records from Thailand and China suggest some lived in freshwater.

cret-055.title: Egg-laying monotremes appear in Australia
cret-055.text: Egg-laying mammals have a record centered on Australia. Teinolophos, which lived about 120 Ma, is one of the earliest known monotremes. Steropodon, from about 105 Ma, has also been called the oldest, and sources give different dates. The only Mesozoic monotremes come from Australia plus Patagonia. Teinolophos is dated Barremian, 126 Ma, and the many Cenomanian forms suggest monotremes were diversifying by the early Late Cretaceous. One hypothesis is that they arose in Australia in the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous and some migrated across the Antarctic land bridge to South America.

cret-057.title: The last mammal-like tritylodontids vanish
cret-057.text: The last animals that were mammal-like but not yet mammals died out in the Early Cretaceous. Herbivorous tritylodontids persisted in Asia into the Barremian–Aptian, at least until around 120 Ma, as Fossiomanus from China shows. They were the last surviving non-mammaliaform cynodonts. Only two groups of non-mammaliaform cynodonts survived past the end of the Triassic, both in Probainognathia. A Kayentatherium specimen shows that tritylodontids already had a marsupial-like reproductive style but produced much larger litters, around 38 perinates or possibly eggs.

cret-064.title: Subduction zones begin to ring the Pacific
cret-064.text:
By about 115 Ma, today's subduction zones had begun to form the Pacific Ring of Fire around South America, North America and Asia. About 120–115 Ma the Farallon plate was subducting beneath the Americas and north-east Asia, and the Izanagi plate beneath east Asia. By 85 to 70 million years ago the Izanagi plate was subducting under east Asia and North America, while the Farallon plate went under South America.

The ring has a gap. It does not cross the southern Pacific from New Zealand to the Antarctic Peninsula or the southern tip of South America. The plate boundaries there (the Pacific–Antarctic Ridge, East Pacific Rise and Chile Ridge) are divergent instead of convergent.

cret-065.title: Vista Alegre crater scars Brazil's basalts
cret-065.text: An impact crater in the basalts of southern Brazil has recently been dated to about 115 Ma. The Vista Alegre crater is a meteorite crater in Coronel Vivida, Paraná State. Given their proximity, age and stratigraphic similarities, it has been proposed that it and the nearby Vargeão structure formed as a double impact. An earlier estimate put the age at Paleogene or younger.

cret-083.title: Meridiolestidans, South America's forgotten mammal rulers
cret-083.text: South America's Late Cretaceous mammals were not the ones we expect. Meridiolestidans were dominant, from sabre-toothed Cronopio to herbivorous mesungulatids. Meridiolestida is an extinct clade known from the Cretaceous and Cenozoic of South America and possibly Antarctica. The group lingered until the Miocene in Patagonia. Dryolestids are known from the Jurassic through Early Cretaceous of the Northern Hemisphere and from the Late Cretaceous through the Miocene of South America.

cret-087.title: The Mississippi embayment, cradle of a great delta
cret-087.text: The Mississippi River Delta traces back about 100 Ma, when the Mississippi embayment formed in the Late Cretaceous. This physiographic feature in the south-central United States is part of the Mississippi Alluvial Plain. The embayment became a primary focus of sediment deposition during the Miocene (about 23 to 5.3 million years ago), which built the foundation of the modern delta region.

cret-093.title: The first true crocodilians
cret-093.text: True crocodilians (Crocodylia) evolve around 95 million years ago. One source dates their appearance to 83.5 million years ago in the Campanian. It calls them the closest living relatives of birds, the two groups being the only known survivors of the Archosauria. Their wider total group, Pseudosuchia, appeared about 250 million years ago in the Early Triassic and diversified during the Mesozoic.

cret-094.title: Lebanon's Sannine fossil beds
cret-094.text: Lebanon's Sannine Formation sites at Haqel, Hjoula and al-Nammoura are famous Cenomanian Lagerstätten, rock deposits with exceptionally preserved fossils. Shrimp, octopus, stingrays and bony fish are common finds, though fossil octopuses are among the rarest. Together with Sahel Alma, these localities are known as the Fish Beds of Lebanon. The formation and its fossil fishes have been known since Roman Phoenicia.

cret-096.title: The first mosasaurs slip into the sea
cret-096.text: The first mosasaurs appear around 94 million years ago. They went on to rule the Late Cretaceous oceans, filling the role left by the ichthyosaurs. Mosasaurs breathed air, were powerful swimmers and were well adapted to the warm, shallow inland seas of the Late Cretaceous. They became extinct in the K-Pg event at the end of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago.

cret-101.title: Lava floods across Madagascar
cret-101.text: Lava once covered Madagascar, roughly 1,000,000 km2 of it before erosion. Flood basalts erupted across the island between about 92 and 85 million years ago, by argon–argon dating. Ages run 88–92 million years in the north and 85–88 million years in the south. The basalts consist of lava flows, dykes, sills and intrusions, with plugs, scoria and spatter cones among other volcanic features.

cret-103.title: The earliest ticks
cret-103.text: The earliest examples of ticks appear around 90 million years ago, but the timing of their origin is uncertain. The oldest known tick fossils are around 100 million years old and come from the Cretaceous. A 2019 analysis suggested that the last common ancestor of all living ticks lived around 195 million years ago in the Southern Hemisphere, in what was then Gondwana. Blood-feeding evolved independently at least six times in arthropods during the late Cretaceous. In ticks it is thought to have evolved 120 million years ago.

cret-104.title: The last carnosaurs fall
cret-104.text: The last definitive carnosaur family, the carcharodontosaurids, became extinct in the Turonian around 90 million years ago. Carnosaurs had first appeared in the Middle Jurassic, around 174 million years ago. They are distinguished by large eye sockets, a long narrow skull, and leg and pelvis modifications such as a thigh bone (femur) longer than the shin (tibia). Most former carnosaurs, such as the megalosaurids, spinosaurids and ceratosaurs, have been reclassified as more primitive theropods.
